content: The effects of conjugated estrogens, when administered vaginally, are not influenced by alterations in intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of the hormone. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and close monitoring are advised when using certain medications concurrently. Methylprednisolone can decrease the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens by influencing hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Similarly, metronidazole can increase the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens through the same enzymatic pathway. Both require careful monitoring. Conjugated estrogens, when used vaginally, may reduce the effects of metyrapone through an unspecified mechanism, though the clinical significance is unclear. Miconazole vaginally can increase the levels or effects of conjugated estrogens via CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating caution. Mycophenolate may decrease the effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens through an unknown mechanism, with unclear clinical significance. Nafcillin decreases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring close monitoring. Nefazodone increases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter and CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction is serious, and alternative drugs should be considered. Nelfinavir increases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring caution. Nevirapine decreases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens through the same pathway, also requiring monitoring. Nicardipine increases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein efflux transporter, necessitating caution. Nifedipine has a dual effect, increasing levels via CYP3A4 metabolism and decreasing levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Nilotinib increases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens through both CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein inhibition, requiring close monitoring. Nilutamide also increases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via CYP3A4 metabolism. Conjugated estrogens may reduce the effects of tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) like nortriptyline, while increasing TCA plasma concentrations and adverse effects. Ospemifene and conjugated estrogens may enhance each other’s effects through pharmacodynamic synergy, requiring therapy modification and monitoring. Oxcarbazepine decreases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via CYP3A4 metabolism. Pentobarbital and phenobarbital decrease the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens through CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein inhibition. Phenytoin similarly decreases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via these pathways. If estrogens are used for contraception, loss of contraceptive efficacy may occur. Phytoestrogens and pleurisy root may decrease the effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens through pharmacodynamic antagonism or unspecified mechanisms, though the clinical significance is unclear. Posaconazole increases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via CYP3A4 metabolism. Prednisone decreases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens through the same pathway. Primidone decreases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via CYP3A4 metabolism. Natural progesterone and conjugated estrogens may interact synergistically, potentially causing breast tenderness. Conjugated estrogens may reduce the effects of protamine through pharmacodynamic antagonism, increasing the risk of thromboembolic disorders. Quercetin decreases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Quinidine increases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens through the same mechanism, requiring alternative drug use. Quinupristin/dalfopristin increases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via CYP3A4 metabolism. Ranolazine increases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Rifabutin and rifampin decrease the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens through CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein inhibition, necessitating alternative drugs. Rifapentine also decreases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via CYP3A4 metabolism. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens through both CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein inhibition. Conjugated estrogens may increase ropinirole levels through an unspecified mechanism. They may also decrease rose hips levels by increasing elimination. Rufinamide decreases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via CYP3A4 metabolism. Simvastatin and sirolimus increase the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Conjugated estrogens may reduce the effects of somapacitan, potentially requiring higher somapacitan dosages. St. John’s Wort decreases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein inhibition, requiring alternative drugs. Tacrolimus and teniposide increase the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Tesamorelin decreases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens by altering metabolism. Tolvaptan increases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Topiramate decreases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via CYP3A4 metabolism. Trazodone decreases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Verapamil increases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein inhibition. Voriconazole increases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens via CYP3A4 metabolism. Zafirlukast increases the levels or effects of vaginal conjugated estrogens through the same pathway. Common adverse effects of conjugated estrogens include abdominal pain, dizziness, breast enlargement, and urinary urgency. Genitourinary effects may include abnormal uterine bleeding, dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, uterine leiomyoma enlargement, vaginitis, and endometrial hyperplasia or cancer. Breast-related effects include tenderness, enlargement, pain, discharge, and fibrocystic changes. Cardiovascular risks include deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), myocardial infarction (MI), and stroke. Gastrointestinal effects include nausea, vomiting, and gallbladder disease. Skin effects include chloasma, hair loss, and rash. Central nervous system effects include headache, migraine, depression, and mood disturbances. Conjugated estrogens are contraindicated in women with undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding, breast cancer, estrogen-dependent neoplasia, active DVT, PE, arterial thromboembolic disease, liver dysfunction, or known thrombophilic disorders. They should not be used during pregnancy. Estrogens may increase the risk of cardiovascular disease, endometrial cancer, breast cancer, and dementia. They may also exacerbate conditions such as asthma, diabetes, epilepsy, and lupus. Estrogens should be discontinued at least 4-6 weeks before surgery associated with thromboembolism risk or during prolonged immobilization. Hormone therapy for menopausal symptoms may increase ovarian cancer risk. Retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported, and medication should be discontinued if vision loss or other symptoms occur. Estrogens may cause fluid retention, requiring caution in women with cardiac or renal dysfunction.
